title: Heritage walk in Vijayapura (Bijapur): Gol Gumbaz and beyond
seo_title: Heritage Walk in Vijayapura: Gol Gumbaz, Ibrahim Rauza, Forts
meta_description: Plan a heritage walk in Vijayapura (Bijapur): Gol Gumbaz, Ibrahim Rauza, Jami Masjid, the citadel, Malik-e-Maidan, Bara Kaman, the ASI museum and nearby sites.
summary: A heritage walk in Vijayapura (formerly Bijapur) covers the capital of the Adil Shahi sultans (1490 to 1686): Gol Gumbaz with its whispering gallery, the Ibrahim Rauza tomb complex, the Jami Masjid, the citadel with Gagan Mahal, the Malik-e-Maidan cannon and the unfinished Bara Kaman.

paras: Vijayapura was the capital of the Adil Shahi dynasty, one of the five Deccan sultanates that followed the break-up of the Bahmani kingdom. In the 16th and 17th centuries it was a wealthy court city of perhaps several hundred thousand people, with a style of architecture all its own: bulbous domes on petal bases, slender minarets, deep cornices on carved brackets, and fine stucco. More than fifty protected monuments survive inside and around the city walls.

The city's best-known building, Gol Gumbaz, has one of the largest domes in the world built without internal supports. Ibrahim Rauza, a tomb and mosque pair on a single platform, is often said to have influenced the design of the Taj Mahal. Both are on India's tentative list for UNESCO as part of the Deccan Sultanate monuments, though not yet inscribed. The city's official name changed from Bijapur to Vijayapura in 2014.

The name goes back to Vijayapura, 'city of victory', of the Kalyani Chalukya period (10th to 12th century); temple pillars from that era were reused in some later mosques. The town passed to the Yadavas, then the Delhi Sultanate and the Bahmanis, under whom it was a provincial seat.

Yusuf Adil Khan, a Bahmani governor, declared independence in 1489 to 1490 and founded the Adil Shahi dynasty. His successors fought and allied with Vijayanagara and the other sultanates; Ali Adil Shah I joined the alliance that defeated Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 (see the [Vijayanagara empire](vijayanagara-empire.html) explainer). Ibrahim Adil Shah II (ruled 1580 to 1627) was a patron of music, painting and poetry; Muhammad Adil Shah (1627 to 1656) built Gol Gumbaz. Aurangzeb conquered the city in 1686, and it declined under Mughal, Maratha, Nizam and British rule.

Our explainer on [Indo-Islamic architecture](indo-islamic-architecture.html) sets the Adil Shahi style against Delhi, Gujarat and Bengal, and the lecture [Deccan temple forms and Vesara debates](deccan-temple-forms-vesara-debates.html) covers the earlier temple builders of the same region.

sections.h2: What you see on a Vijayapura heritage walk
paras: At Gol Gumbaz students climb one of the corner towers to the whispering gallery inside the dome, where a whisper carries round to the other side, and look out over the city from the roof. The base is a cube of about 47 metres a side; ask the group to work out how the round dome sits on a square plan using intersecting arches, a neat lesson in structure.

Ibrahim Rauza, on the western edge of town, is the other centre of the walk. The tomb of Ibrahim Adil Shah II and the mosque face each other across a garden platform, with carved stone screens, calligraphy and a flat stone ceiling held up by clever jointing. In between, the citadel (Arkilla) holds Gagan Mahal, Sat Manzil and the Jala Manzil water pavilion, and the Jami Masjid, begun by Ali Adil Shah I around 1576, shows a great congregational mosque in Deccani style.

On the western walls, the Malik-e-Maidan, a bronze cannon cast in Ahmadnagar in 1549 and brought to Bijapur, sits on its bastion. The Taj Bawdi, a large stepped tank, shows how the city managed water. A [heritage photography walk](heritage-photography-evidence-led-photo-walk.html) works well across these varied sites.

sections.h2: Planning a Vijayapura heritage walk for schools and groups
paras: The monuments are spread across a walled city about 10 kilometres round, so a group needs a vehicle or auto-rickshaws between clusters, then walks within each. A full day covers the main sites; a second day lets you add Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal, about 2.5 hours south. Gol Gumbaz is busy and noisy by late morning, so arrive early to hear the echo properly.

Vijayapura walks are arranged with your group, at the pace and length you choose. The [Pattadakal and Aihole study day](pattadakal-and-aihole-temple-design-laboratory.html) pairs naturally with a day here, and a [study tour built for your group](a-study-tour-built-for-your-group.html) can join Vijayapura, Badami and Hampi into one north Karnataka trip.

stops.name: Gol Gumbaz
stops.note: Tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah with a huge dome and whispering gallery; climb the tower stairs.

stops.name: ASI Museum at Gol Gumbaz
stops.note: In the naqqar khana (drum house) in front of the tomb, with inscriptions, manuscripts, arms and sculpture.

stops.name: Jami Masjid
stops.note: Large congregational mosque started by Ali Adil Shah I, with a gilded mihrab.

stops.name: Arkilla (citadel)
stops.note: Inner fort with palaces, gardens and a moat.

stops.name: Gagan Mahal
stops.note: Audience hall with a very wide central arch facing the city.

stops.name: Jala Manzil and Sat Manzil
stops.note: A water pavilion and the remains of a seven-storey palace in the citadel.

stops.name: Bara Kaman
stops.note: Arches of a planned tomb of Ali Adil Shah II that was never completed.

stops.name: Mehtar Mahal
stops.note: Ornate gateway with carved stone balconies and brackets leading to a small mosque.

stops.name: Ibrahim Rauza
stops.note: Tomb and mosque of Ibrahim Adil Shah II on one platform, with fine carving and calligraphy.

stops.name: Malik-e-Maidan
stops.note: Bronze cannon on the Sherza Burj bastion of the city walls.

stops.name: Upli Burj
stops.note: Tall watchtower with two cannons and a view over the city.

stops.name: Taj Bawdi
stops.note: Large stepped water tank built in honour of Taj Sultana, a queen of Ibrahim II.

routes.name: Gol Gumbaz and the east (short drives)
Walls and Ibrahim Rauza (vehicle between stops)

museums.name: ASI Archaeological Museum, Gol Gumbaz
museums.note: Arabic and Persian inscriptions, Chalukya sculpture, manuscripts, carpets, porcelain and arms of the Adil Shahi court.

museums.name: Site interpretation at Ibrahim Rauza
museums.note: ASI signboards explaining the plan and construction of the complex.

best_time: October to February. Summers in north Karnataka are very hot; start by 8 am at any time of year.

faq.q: What are the main historical places in Vijayapura?
faq.a: Gol Gumbaz, Ibrahim Rauza, the Jami Masjid, the citadel with Gagan Mahal, Bara Kaman, Mehtar Mahal, Malik-e-Maidan, Upli Burj and Taj Bawdi, plus the ASI museum at Gol Gumbaz.

faq.q: Is Bijapur the same as Vijayapura?
faq.a: Yes. The city's official name changed from Bijapur to Vijayapura in 2014. Many books and older maps still use Bijapur.
It is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, finished around 1656, with one of the largest unsupported domes in the world and a whispering gallery where a quiet sound carries across the dome.

faq.q: Is Vijayapura a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.a: Not yet. The monuments of the Deccan sultanates, including those at Vijayapura, are on India's tentative list but have not been inscribed.

faq.q: Do I need a vehicle for a Vijayapura heritage walk?
faq.a: Yes, between clusters. The walled city is large, so groups drive between Gol Gumbaz, the citadel and Ibrahim Rauza, and walk within each.

bundle.pitch: A day in the Adil Shahi capital, then a day in the Chalukya temple towns of Aihole and Pattadakal: two very different ways of building in the same region.

posts.hook: Whisper in Gol Gumbaz and it comes back across the dome.
posts.caption: Completed around 1656 for Muhammad Adil Shah, the dome is one of the largest built without internal supports. The gallery inside carries the softest sound right around.

posts.hook: Get to Gol Gumbaz before 9 am.
posts.caption: Later in the day the gallery fills with people shouting to test the echo. Early, you can hear a whisper the way it was meant to carry.
